lessons.title: Finding buyers: local traders, breweries, schools, and NGOs
lessons.body:
Your sorghum and millet harvest is money waiting to happen, but only if you find the right buyer. Start with local traders at your nearest market. They buy in bulk and pay cash, but prices are often low. Visit the market on different days to learn who pays best. For example, in many parts of Nigeria, a trader might offer â¦25,000 per 100kg bag of sorghum, while another offers â¦28,000. Always ask around before selling.

Breweries are a major buyer for sorghum. Companies like Nigerian Breweries, Guinness, and SABMiller use sorghum for beer and malt drinks. They often contract farmers directly, providing seeds and buying the harvest. Contact their local office or agricultural department to ask about contract farming. They require clean, high-quality grain, so proper drying and storage matter. Payment is usually by bank transfer after delivery.

Schools and universities with boarding facilities buy millet and sorghum for porridge and meals. Approach the school bursar or catering officer with a sample and your price. They prefer consistent supply and may sign a term contract. NGOs and food aid organisations also buy for relief programmes. For instance, the World Food Programme (WFP) purchases locally from smallholder farmers. Register with farmer groups or check tender notices in district offices.

Don't ignore local processors who make flour, beverages, or animal feed. They may buy regularly. To find all these buyers, attend agricultural shows, join farmer associations, and use radio announcements. Keep a list of buyers with their contact details and typical prices. Always get a written agreement or receipt for large sales. Building relationships with several buyers reduces risk. Never rely on one buyer; if they delay payment or lower prices, you have alternatives.

lessons.title: Negotiating prices and understanding market cycles
lessons.body:
Negotiating a good price starts with knowing the market. Sorghum and millet prices follow seasonal cycles. Right after harvest, when many farmers sell, prices drop. For example, in Burkina Faso, millet might sell for 150 CFA francs per kg at harvest, but rise to 250 CFA francs per kg during the lean season (June-August). If you can store your grain safely, you can sell later for more. But storage costs and spoilage risk must be considered.

Before you negotiate, check current prices. Use your mobile phone to call other farmers, traders, or listen to market radio programmes. In Kenya, the Kenya Agricultural Commodity Exchange (KACE) sends SMS price alerts. In Ghana, Esoko provides similar services. Knowing the price gives you confidence. When a trader offers a low price, you can say, 'I know the price at Techiman market is 200 cedis per bag; can you match that?'

Negotiation is not a fight; it's a conversation. Be polite but firm. Start by asking the buyer's best price, then counter with a slightly higher figure. Be ready to walk away if the offer is too low. If you have quality grain, emphasise that: 'My sorghum is well-dried and clean, no stones or mould. That's worth a premium.' For large volumes, ask for a better price per bag. Also discuss payment terms: cash on delivery is best. If they want credit, agree on a written date and possibly a higher price to cover risk.

Market cycles also depend on demand from breweries, schools, and export. For instance, when breweries increase production, sorghum demand rises. Keep informed through farmer groups and extension officers. Plan to sell when prices are high, but don't hold too long if you need cash. A good strategy: sell half at harvest to cover immediate costs, store half for later. Always calculate your cost of production to know your minimum price. Never sell below that.

lessons.title: Grading and sorting for premium prices
lessons.body:
Grading and sorting your sorghum and millet can increase your income by 10-30%. Buyers pay more for clean, uniform grain. Start by removing foreign matter: stones, sand, chaff, and damaged grains. Use a simple sieve or winnowing basket. For millet, you can also use a destoner. After cleaning, sort by size and colour. For sorghum, uniform red or white grains are preferred. For millet, uniform pearl or finger millet grains.

Different grades have different prices. For example, Grade 1 sorghum (less than 1% foreign matter, moisture below 12%) might sell for 20% more than Grade 3. Breweries and processors often specify grade standards. Ask your buyer for their requirements. Common grades: Grade 1 for premium food and brewing, Grade 2 for general food, Grade 3 for animal feed. Use a moisture meter to check dryness; if you don't have one, bite a grainâit should be hard and crack, not soft.

Packaging also matters. Use clean, new bags (50kg or 100kg). Label with your name, grade, and weight. For premium markets, you might pack in 1kg or 5kg branded bags for direct sale to consumers. This adds value but requires investment in packaging and marketing. Start small: sell graded grain in bulk to traders and processors, then explore value addition later.

To get the best price, take samples to buyers before delivery. Let them see the quality. If they agree to a higher price, deliver the same quality. Consistency builds trust. Join a cooperative to access better grading equipment and training. Many NGOs and projects offer grading and sorting workshops. Invest a little time in cleaning; the returns are worth it. Remember, a clean product opens doors to high-value buyers like breweries and export markets.

lessons.title: Using mobile phones and apps to check market prices
lessons.body:
Your mobile phone is a powerful marketing tool. You can check market prices without leaving your farm. In many African countries, there are services that send price information via SMS or USSD. For example, in Kenya, dial *654# to access M-Farm, which gives prices for maize, sorghum, and other crops. In Ghana, Esoko offers a similar service. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Commodity Exchange has price updates. Ask your extension officer or fellow farmers about the service in your area.

Smartphone apps are also available. Download apps like 'Farmerline' (Ghana), 'Kilimo Salama' (Kenya), or 'AgriApp' (Nigeria). These apps show prices from different markets. They also provide weather forecasts and farming tips. If you don't have a smartphone, you can still use SMS. For instance, send a text to a short code with the crop name and market, and receive the current price. Some services charge a small fee per message, but it's worth it.

Beyond apps, use social media. Join WhatsApp or Telegram groups for farmers in your region. Members often share prices and buyer requests. Facebook groups like 'Sorghum Farmers Association of Nigeria' can be useful. You can also call traders directly to ask their price. Build a network of contacts: other farmers, traders, extension officers, and cooperative leaders. They are your eyes and ears.

When you have price information, compare across markets. Sometimes it's worth transporting to a distant market if the price difference covers transport costs. For example, if sorghum is 200 birr per quintal in your village and 250 birr in the next town, and transport costs 30 birr per quintal, you gain 20 birr. Use simple arithmetic. Also, check prices regularly to understand trends. Keep a notebook or use your phone's notes app to record prices weekly. Over time, you'll know when to sell. Remember, information is power; the more you know, the better you negotiate.

lessons.title: Forming or joining a farmer cooperative for better sales
lessons.body:
A farmer cooperative is a group of farmers who work together to buy inputs, share knowledge, and sell their harvest. Joining or forming one can increase your bargaining power. When you sell alone, you might get a low price because traders know you have limited volume. But a cooperative can aggregate hundreds of tonnes, attracting big buyers like breweries and NGOs. For example, the Sorghum Farmers Cooperative in Kano, Nigeria, sells directly to Nigerian Breweries at a premium price.

To form a cooperative, start with at least 10-15 farmers in your area. Hold a meeting to discuss goals and rules. Elect leaders: chairperson, secretary, treasurer. Register with the government's cooperative department to get legal status. This allows you to open a bank account and sign contracts. Many NGOs and government programmes provide training and grants to new cooperatives. For instance, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) supports cooperative development in many African countries.

As a member, you benefit in several ways. You can access bulk inputs like improved seeds and fertiliser at lower prices. You can share equipment like threshers and storage facilities. You can get training on grading, post-harvest handling, and marketing. When selling, the cooperative negotiates as one. They can demand higher prices, arrange transport, and ensure timely payment. Some cooperatives also add value by processing flour or packaging for retail.

But cooperatives require commitment. You must follow the rules, contribute fees, and attend meetings. There may be challenges like mismanagement or delayed payments. Choose leaders wisely and demand transparency. If you prefer not to join, you can still collaborate informally with neighbours to sell together. But a formal cooperative opens more doors. Check with your local extension officer about existing cooperatives in your area. Joining one is often easier than starting from scratch. Remember, unity is strength; together you can get better prices and services.

lessons.title: Transport and logistics: reducing post-harvest losses to market
lessons.body:
Getting your harvest to market without losses is crucial. Post-harvest losses for sorghum and millet can be 10-20% if not handled well. Losses happen during harvesting, drying, storage, and transport. To reduce them, start with proper drying. Dry your grain to below 12% moisture before storage. Use a moisture meter or the salt test: mix salt with grain in a bottle, shake, and if salt sticks, it's too wet. Dry on a clean tarpaulin, not on the ground, to avoid contamination.

For storage, use hermetic bags like Purdue Improved Crop Storage (PICS) bags. These bags kill insects without chemicals and keep grain safe for months. They cost about $2-3 each and can store 100kg. Alternatively, use metal silos or clean drums with tight lids. Add a layer of ash or neem leaves to deter pests. Never store grain on the floor; use pallets to avoid moisture. Check regularly for signs of insects or mould.

When transporting, use clean, dry bags. Don't overload vehicles; stack bags properly to avoid tearing. Cover with tarpaulin if it might rain. For short distances, use a bicycle or motorcycle with a carrier. For longer distances, hire a truck. If you're part of a cooperative, you can hire a truck together, reducing costs. For example, a 10-tonne truck from Kano to Lagos might cost â¦200,000, but shared among 20 farmers, it's affordable.

Plan your transport to avoid delays. Harvest when dry, and sell when roads are passable. In rainy season, roads may be bad, increasing costs and losses. Consider selling to a nearby market if transport is risky. Always get a receipt for transport and keep records. If you deliver to a buyer, ensure they inspect and accept the grain before unloading. Any rejected grain must be brought back or sold elsewhere. Reducing losses means more money in your pocket. Invest in good bags and storage; it pays off.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Marketing and Selling Your Sorghum & Millet Harvest

Sorghum and millet are no longer just subsistence crops. Across the Sahel, East Africa, and Southern Africa, demand is rising from breweries, feed mills, schools, NGOs, and urban consumers who want gluten-free and climate-smart grains. But producing a good harvest is only half the business. The money is made â or lost â in how you find buyers, negotiate, grade, and move your grain to market. This practical reference gives you the tools, numbers, and checklists to turn your sorghum and millet into reliable income.

1. Finding Buyers: Local Traders, Breweries, Schools, and NGOs

Your first step is to map every possible buyer within reach. There are four main buyer categories, and each has different price, volume, and payment behaviour.

  • Local traders and aggregators: They buy in small volumes, pay cash quickly, but often offer the lowest price. Good for immediate cash flow after harvest.
  • Breweries and processors: Companies such as East African Breweries, SABMiller/AB InBev, and local millers buy sorghum in bulk for clear beer, porridge flour, and animal feed. They pay premium prices but require consistent quality, volume, and formal contracts.
  • Schools, hospitals, and institutions: They buy millet and sorghum for school feeding programmes and patient meals. Contracts are often seasonal and require reliable delivery.
  • NGOs and relief agencies: WFP, FAO, and local NGOs buy for food assistance. They pay well but demand strict quality standards, traceability, and sometimes certification.

Business tip: Do not rely on one buyer. Sell 60% to a contract buyer (brewery or institution) for stable income, and 40% to local traders for flexibility and quick cash.

2. Negotiating Prices and Understanding Market Cycles

Prices for sorghum and millet follow predictable seasonal cycles. Immediately after harvest (typically OctoberâDecember in the Sahel, JuneâAugust in East Africa), supply floods the market and prices drop 20â40%. By the lean season (MarchâJuly), prices can double. The business skill is to sell part of your harvest at harvest for cash flow, and store the rest to sell when prices rise.

Negotiation rules:

  • Never accept the first offer. Ask for 15â20% above the quoted price and negotiate down.
  • Know the current market price before you negotiate. Use mobile apps (see section 4).
  • Sell in graded, uniform lots â buyers pay more for clean, sorted grain.
  • Negotiate volume discounts for buyers who take larger quantities.
  • Get payment terms in writing: cash on delivery, 7-day, or 30-day payment.
Table 1: Typical sorghum and millet price ranges by buyer type (USD per 100 kg, 2023â2024)
Buyer Type Sorghum (USD/100kg) Millet (USD/100kg) Payment Speed Quality Requirements
Local trader (farmgate) 18â25 22â30 Immediate cash Low â any condition
Local market (retail) 25â35 30â42 Immediate cash Medium â cleaned
Brewery (contract) 32â45 N/A (rare) 7â30 days High â specific variety, moisture <12%
School / NGO 28â40 35â48 14â30 days High â aflatoxin tested, clean
Processor / miller 30â42 38â50 7â21 days Medium-high â uniform grain

Sources: FAO Food Price Monitoring (2024); East African Grain Council market reports (2023); Sahel Grains Network price bulletins (2024). Prices vary by country and season.

3. Grading and Sorting for Premium Prices

Grading is the single cheapest way to increase your income. A farmer who sells unsorted grain may receive 20â30% less than one who sells clean, graded, uniform lots. Buyers pay for consistency â they need to know that every bag meets the same standard.

Grading steps:

  1. Clean: Remove stones, sand, chaff, and foreign matter. Use a sieve or winnowing.
  2. Sort: Remove broken, discoloured, and mouldy grains. These lower the entire lot's value.
  3. Dry: Ensure moisture content is below 12â13% for safe storage and premium pricing.
  4. Grade by size and colour: Uniform grain commands higher prices, especially for breweries.
  5. Package: Use clean, labelled bags (50 kg or 100 kg). Brand your bags with your cooperative name.
Table 2: Grading standards and price premiums for sorghum and millet in African markets
Grade Criteria Price Premium vs. Ungraded Best Buyer
Grade A (Premium) <1% foreign matter, <12% moisture, uniform colour, no broken grains +25â35% Breweries, NGOs, processors
Grade B (Standard) <3% foreign matter, <13% moisture, minor colour variation +10â20% Schools, millers, urban retail
Grade C (Fair) <5% foreign matter, <14% moisture, some broken grains Base price Local traders, feed mills
Ungraded Mixed, dirty, high moisture â10â20% (discount) Local traders only

Sources: East African Community (EAC) Grain Standards (2022); FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius for sorghum and millet (2021); Africa Grain Council grading guidelines (2023).

4. Using Mobile Phones and Apps to Check Market Prices

Information is power. Farmers with access to real-time market prices negotiate 10â25% better prices than those without. Several free and low-cost tools are available across Africa:

  • MFarm (Kenya): SMS and app-based market prices for grains, including sorghum and millet.
  • Esoko (Ghana, Nigeria, and West Africa): Provides commodity prices, weather, and buyer connections via SMS.
  • Agri-Business Africa / Kilimo (Tanzania): Market price alerts and buyer directories.
  • WhatsApp and Telegram groups: Many cooperatives and traders run price-sharing groups. Join local grain trader groups.
  • Radio and SMS: Even without a smartphone, you can subscribe to SMS price alerts from national bureaus of statistics or agricultural ministries.

How to use price information: Check prices weekly. Compare at least three sources. When you know the market price, you can confidently reject low offers and time your sales.

5. Forming or Joining a Farmer Cooperative for Better Sales

Individual farmers selling 500 kg cannot access brewery contracts or NGO tenders. Cooperatives aggregate volume, improve bargaining power, and reduce transaction costs. A cooperative of 50 farmers with 50 tonnes of sorghum can negotiate 30â50% higher prices than individual farmers.

Steps to form or join a cooperative:

  1. Register with the national cooperative authority (e.g., Kenya's Commissioner for Cooperatives, Nigeria's Federal Department of Cooperatives).
  2. Elect a management committee and a treasurer. Open a bank account.
  3. Set quality standards and a grading system for all members.
  4. Appoint a marketing officer to contact buyers and negotiate contracts.
  5. Pool transport and storage to reduce costs.
  6. Share profits based on volume and quality delivered â not equally.

6. Transport and Logistics: Reducing Post-Harvest Losses to Market

Post-harvest losses for sorghum and millet in Africa range from 10â30%, according to FAO. Most losses happen during transport, storage, and handling. Reducing these losses is directly equivalent to increasing your income.

  • Use clean, dry bags: Never transport grain in dirty or wet sacks. Use polypropylene bags with liners for moisture protection.
  • Load carefully: Avoid overloading. Use tarpaulins to protect from rain and dust.
  • Transport during dry hours: Early morning or late afternoon to avoid heat and rain.
  • Store properly: Use raised pallets, hermetic storage bags (e.g., Purdue Improved Crop Storage â PICS bags), and keep storage dry and ventilated.
  • Pool transport: Cooperatives can hire a truck for 10 tonnes and share costs, reducing per-bag transport cost by 40â60%.
  • Insure your load: For large volumes, consider transport insurance against accidents and theft.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Aflatoxin and Moisture

Never sell or transport grain with moisture above 14% or with visible mould. Sorghum and millet can develop aflatoxin â a poisonous substance that causes liver cancer and stunting in children. Buyers in formal markets (breweries, NGOs, schools) will reject contaminated grain and may blacklist you. Always dry grain to below 12â13% moisture before storage or sale. Test with a moisture meter if available. If grain smells musty or shows green/yellow mould, do not sell it for human consumption â use it for animal feed only after testing, or discard it. Your reputation is your most valuable business asset.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Identify at least 4 buyers: local trader, brewery/processor, school/NGO, cooperative.
  • â Check market prices weekly via mobile apps, SMS, or radio before negotiating.
  • â Grade and sort every lot â clean, dry, uniform grain earns 20â35% more.
  • â Dry grain to below 12â13% moisture and test for aflatoxin before selling.
  • â Sell 60% on contract and 40% on spot market for balanced income.
  • â Join or form a cooperative to access bulk buyers and share transport costs.
  • â Use clean, dry, labelled bags and cover loads with tarpaulins during transport.
  • â Get all payment terms in writing â never rely on verbal agreements.

Further Reading

  • FAO Markets and Trade â global and regional food market information, including sorghum and millet.
  • World Food Programme (WFP) Purchase for Progress â how smallholder farmers can sell to WFP and its partners.
  • Africa Grain Council â grading standards, market reports, and buyer directories.
  • East African Grain Council (EAGC) â regional market prices, standards, and trade facilitation.
  • IFAD Rural Development â cooperative formation, rural finance, and market access guidance.

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills programme. All prices and standards are indicative and may vary by country and season. Always verify with local market authorities and buyer contracts.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a major buyer of sorghum for brewing?
quiz.explanation: Nigerian Breweries and similar companies use sorghum for beer production.

quiz.q: What is a good way to find buyers for your sorghum and millet?
options: A) Wait for them to come to you
quiz.explanation: Agricultural shows connect farmers with various buyers and provide market information.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a list of buyers?
options: B) To have alternatives if one delays payment
C) To increase your social status
quiz.explanation: Having multiple buyers reduces risk and gives you options if one buyer fails.

quiz.q: When do sorghum and millet prices typically drop?
quiz.explanation: After harvest, supply is high, so prices fall due to increased market volume.

quiz.q: What is a good strategy to take advantage of market cycles?
options: B) Store half and sell later
quiz.explanation: Storing part of the harvest allows you to sell when prices rise during the lean season.

quiz.q: Which service provides SMS price alerts for crops in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: M-Farm is a Kenyan service that sends market prices via SMS.

quiz.q: What should you do before negotiating a price?
quiz.explanation: Knowing current prices gives you confidence and a basis for negotiation.

quiz.q: What is a key factor in negotiating a better price?
quiz.explanation: Quality grain justifies a higher price, so highlight it during negotiations.

quiz.q: Why is it important to know your cost of production?
options: A) To know your minimum selling price
quiz.explanation: Knowing costs helps you set a floor price below which you shouldn't sell.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of grading and sorting your grain?
options: B) It can increase price by 10-30%
quiz.explanation: Clean, uniform grain is more valuable and can fetch premium prices.

quiz.q: What is a common grade standard for sorghum?
options: A) Grade 1: less than 1% foreign matter
quiz.explanation: Grade 1 sorghum has minimal foreign matter and low moisture, ideal for premium markets.

quiz.q: How can you check if your grain is dry enough for storage?
options: B) Bite a grain; it should crack
quiz.explanation: Dry grain is hard and cracks when bitten, indicating low moisture.

quiz.q: What packaging is recommended for premium markets?
options: B) Clean, new bags with labels
quiz.explanation: Clean, labelled bags present your product well and meet buyer requirements.

quiz.q: Why is consistency in quality important?
options: A) It builds trust with buyers
B) It allows you to cheat
quiz.explanation: Consistent quality ensures repeat business and better prices.

quiz.q: What mobile phone service can help you check market prices in Ghana?
quiz.explanation: Esoko is a Ghanaian platform providing agricultural market information via mobile.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using USSD codes for price checks?
options: A) They work on any phone
D) They only work on smartphones
quiz.explanation: USSD codes work on basic phones without internet, making them accessible to all farmers.

quiz.q: How can social media help in marketing?
options: A) By sharing prices and buyer requests
quiz.explanation: Farmer groups on WhatsApp and Facebook share market information and leads.

quiz.q: When comparing prices across markets, what must you consider?
options: D) The colour of the market
quiz.explanation: Transport costs can eat into profits, so calculate if the price difference is worth it.

quiz.q: What is a farmer cooperative?
options: A) A group of farmers working together
quiz.explanation: A cooperative is a farmer-led organisation for mutual benefit in marketing and input purchase.

quiz.q: How does a cooperative increase bargaining power?
quiz.explanation: Larger volumes attract big buyers and better prices.

quiz.q: What is needed to register a cooperative?
quiz.explanation: Most cooperatives require a minimum number of members to register.

quiz.q: What is a potential challenge of cooperatives?
quiz.explanation: Poor leadership or lack of transparency can hinder cooperative success.

quiz.q: What is a hermetic storage bag?
options: A) A bag that kills insects without chemicals
B) A bag made of cloth
C) A bag that attracts moisture
D) A bag for transport only
quiz.explanation: Hermetic bags like PICS create an airtight environment that kills pests.

quiz.q: How can you reduce post-harvest losses during storage?
quiz.explanation: Pallets keep grain off the floor, preventing moisture absorption.

quiz.q: What is the recommended moisture level for safe storage of sorghum?
quiz.explanation: Grain with less than 12% moisture is safe from mould and insects.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid overloading transport vehicles?
options: A) To prevent bag tearing and losses
quiz.explanation: Overloading can damage bags and cause grain spillage, increasing losses.

quiz.q: What is a cost-effective transport option for small quantities?
quiz.explanation: For short distances and small volumes, bicycles or motorcycles are affordable.

quiz.q: How can a cooperative reduce transport costs?
options: A) By hiring a truck together
B) By each farmer hiring their own
quiz.explanation: Sharing a truck among members lowers individual transport expenses.

quiz.q: What should you do if a buyer rejects your grain at delivery?
options: A) Bring it back or sell elsewhere
quiz.explanation: Rejected grain should be taken back to avoid total loss and sold to another buyer.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records of transport and sales?
options: A) To track costs and profits
quiz.explanation: Records help you analyse your business and make better decisions.
